section.title: The Altar and the Courtyard
section.sectionRationale: Moving outward from the tabernacle's inner furnishings, God now gives the pattern for the bronze altar of sacrifice and the surrounding courtyard, the outer boundary that every worshiper must cross, along with the command to keep a lamp burning continually before the LORD.
section.thesis: God instructs Moses to build a bronze altar for burnt offerings and a linen-walled courtyard around the tabernacle, and commands that pure oil keep the lamp burning before Him continually, from evening until morning.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the bronze altar of burnt offering with its horns and utensils; the courtyard of linen curtains enclosing the tabernacle; and the command for continual oil to keep the lamp burning.

media.alt: A bronze altar with horns at its corners
media.caption: The bronze altar of burnt offering stands at the entrance to the courtyard.

verses.text: “You are to build an {{altar|altar}} of acacia wood. The altar must be square, five cubits long, five cubits wide, and three cubits high.
Make a horn on each of its four corners, so that the horns are of one piece, and overlay it with bronze.
Make all its utensils of bronze, its pots for removing ashes, its shovels, its sprinkling bowls, its meat forks, and its firepans.
Construct for it a grate of bronze mesh, and make a bronze ring at each of the four corners of the mesh.
Set the grate beneath the ledge of the altar, so that the mesh comes halfway up the altar.
Additionally, make poles of acacia wood for the altar and overlay them with bronze.
The poles are to be inserted into the rings so that the poles are on two sides of the altar when it is carried.
Construct the altar with boards so that it is hollow. It is to be made just as you were shown on the mountain.

units.label: The courtyard
units.note: a hundred cubits long, fifty cubits wide

verses.text: You are also to make a courtyard for the tabernacle. On the south side of the courtyard make curtains of finely spun linen, a hundred cubits long on one side,
with twenty posts and twenty bronze bases, and silver hooks and bands on the posts.
Likewise there are to be curtains on the north side, a hundred cubits long, with twenty posts and twenty bronze bases, and with silver hooks and bands on the posts.
The curtains on the west side of the courtyard shall be fifty cubits wide, with ten posts and ten bases.
The east side of the courtyard, toward the sunrise, is to be fifty cubits wide.
Make the curtains on one side fifteen cubits long, with three posts and three bases,
and the curtains on the other side fifteen cubits long, with three posts and three bases.
The gate of the courtyard shall be twenty cubits long, with a curtain embroidered with blue, purple, and scarlet yarn, and finely spun linen. It shall have four posts and four bases.
All the posts around the courtyard shall have silver bands, silver hooks, and bronze bases.
The entire courtyard shall be a hundred cubits long and fifty cubits wide, with curtains of finely spun linen five cubits high, and with bronze bases.
All the utensils of the tabernacle for every use, including all its tent pegs and the tent pegs of the courtyard, shall be made of bronze.
And you are to command the Israelites to bring you pure oil of pressed olives for the light, to keep the lamps burning {{continually|continually}}.

In the Tent of Meeting, outside the veil that is in front of the Testimony, Aaron and his sons are to tend the lamps before the LORD from evening until morning. This is to be a permanent statute for the Israelites for the generations to come.

altar.gloss: Altar, from the root meaning to slaughter or sacrifice. This bronze altar stood at the entrance to the tabernacle courtyard, the first thing any worshiper encountered, since approach to God always required a sacrifice for sin.

continually.gloss: Continually, perpetually, without interruption. Used of the lamp that must never go out, this word marks several ongoing tabernacle practices, emphasizing that Israel's worship and God's provision for it were meant to be unceasing, not occasional.

basic.context: God now describes the bronze altar of sacrifice, the very first structure any Israelite would meet on entering the tabernacle courtyard, along with the linen walls of the courtyard itself and the command to keep a lamp burning continually before Him. Sacrifice comes before access; the outer boundary comes before the inner sanctuary.
basic.hermeneutics: These are literal building instructions for Israel's worship space, not abstract symbols to be mined for hidden meaning. The order matters here as much as the details: a worshiper met the altar of sacrifice before anything else, showing that atonement for sin was the very first requirement of approaching a holy God.
basic.originalLanguages: The mizbeach, altar, takes its name from the verb to slaughter, since sacrifice for sin stood at the very entrance to worship. The lamp was to burn tamid, continually, a small but constant reminder that God's provision and Israel's worship were never meant to lapse.
basic.typology: The bronze altar, standing between the worshiper and the tabernacle itself, points to Christ's sacrifice as the necessary first step of approach to God; no one bypasses the altar to reach the Holy Place. The continually burning lamp anticipates the unceasing light and life believers have in Christ.
basic.christ: Hebrews 13:10 speaks of believers having an altar, pointing to Christ's once for all sacrifice, which the bronze altar's repeated offerings could only foreshadow. Where this altar required constant, repeated sacrifice, Christ's single sacrifice accomplishes forever what these offerings could never finish, Hebrews 10:11-14.
basic.god: God places the altar of sacrifice first, before any other furnishing, making plain that sinful people cannot approach Him without atonement. Yet He also commands a light kept burning continually, showing His unbroken commitment to remain present and provide for His people's ongoing worship.
basic.crossReferences: Hebrews 10:11-14 contrasts the repeated sacrifices at this altar with Christ's single, sufficient sacrifice. Hebrews 13:10 speaks of an altar believers now have in Christ. Leviticus 24:1-4 repeats the command for continually burning lamps.
basic.oneStory: Before Israel could approach God's dwelling, they had to pass the altar of sacrifice, a constant reminder that sin must be atoned for. That altar, offered again and again, points forward to the one sacrifice of Christ, who opens the way to God once for all and keeps His light burning for His people forever.

context.literary:
Exodus 27 completes the outward movement that began with the ark in chapter 25. The instructions have travelled from the Most Holy Place, through the Holy Place and the tent, and now reach the open court where every Israelite could stand. The chapter has three parts: the altar, verses 1 to 8, the courtyard, verses 9 to 19, and the oil for the lamp, verses 20 and 21.

The altar section follows the same pattern as the furnishings of chapter 25: wood, overlay, rings, poles, and a closing reminder, 'It is to be made just as you were shown on the mountain,' verse 8. But the metal has changed. Inside the tent everything was gold. Out here the altar, its utensils, the bases of the courtyard posts and even the tent pegs are bronze, verses 2, 3, 17 and 19, with silver used only for the hooks and bands. The descent from gold to silver to bronze maps the movement from the centre of holiness to its edge.

The altar is also the largest single furnishing described so far, five cubits square and three high, twice the length of the ark. Its size fits its task. Everything else in the sanctuary is approached once this altar has done its work.

The courtyard is described side by side, south, north, west and finally east, where the entrance lies 'toward the sunrise,' verse 13. Only the gate is coloured, with the same blue, purple and scarlet as the tent screen and the veil, verse 16, so that the one way in is also the one place of beauty in an otherwise plain white wall.

The last two verses seem at first to be out of place, since the lampstand was described in chapter 25. But they make a bridge. They introduce Aaron and his sons, verse 21, and so lead straight into the priestly garments of chapter 28 and the ordination of chapter 29. A sanctuary needs priests, and the lamp is their first stated duty.
context.historical:
The bronze altar was a hollow box of acacia boards with bronze overlay, verse 8, light enough to be carried on poles. Many suggest that at each campsite it was filled with earth or stones, which would fit the earlier command for 'an altar of earth,' Exodus 20:24, but the text does not say so. Its dimensions, about seven and a half feet square and four and a half feet high by the footnote's reckoning, made it large enough for the regular burnt offerings of lambs, Exodus 29:38-42, and for larger animals.

Altars with four projecting horns at the corners were used in Israel and among its neighbours, and horned altars have been found by archaeologists at several sites in the land. In Israel the horns received the blood of the sin offering, Leviticus 4:25, and they became a place of refuge. Adonijah and Joab both fled to take hold of 'the horns of the altar,' 1 Kings 1:50 and 2:28, and the law had already made clear that the altar gave no shelter to a deliberate murderer, Exodus 21:14.

The courtyard measured about one hundred and fifty feet by seventy five feet, and its linen walls were five cubits high, about seven and a half feet, verse 18. An adult standing outside could not see in. The white curtain would have stood out sharply against the brown tents of the camp and the desert beyond.

The oil was to be 'pure oil of pressed olives,' verse 20. Olives beaten or pressed gently yield the clearest oil, which burns with less smoke. It was the same quality of oil used with the daily offering, Exodus 29:40. Tending the lamps 'from evening until morning' meant a nightly task for the priests, and 1 Samuel 3:3 recalls a night at Shiloh 'before the lamp of God had gone out.' The lamp, like the altar fire, Leviticus 6:13, was never to be neglected.
context.canonical:
The altar of burnt offering stands at the centre of Israel's worship for the rest of the Old Testament. Solomon builds a bronze altar twenty cubits square, 2 Chronicles 4:1. Ezekiel's vision of the restored temple includes a great altar with four horns, Ezekiel 43:13-17. Fire from the LORD consumes the first offerings on the altar in Leviticus 9:24, and fire falls again at the dedication of Solomon's temple, 2 Chronicles 7:1.

The horns carry weight in poetry and prophecy. The psalmist calls the people to 'bind the festal sacrifice with cords to the horns of the altar,' Psalm 118:27. Amos announces judgment on false worship: 'the horns of the altar will be cut off,' Amos 3:14. The same word for horn becomes an image of strength and salvation, 'the horn of my salvation,' Psalm 18:2, and Zechariah praises God for raising up 'a horn of salvation for us in the house of His servant David,' Luke 1:69.

The courts of God's house become a place of longing: 'better is one day in Your courts than a thousand elsewhere,' Psalm 84:10, and 'Enter His gates with thanksgiving and His courts with praise,' Psalm 100:4. Isaiah is cleansed by a coal 'from the altar,' Isaiah 6:6-7.

In the New Testament Jesus assumes the altar's importance when He tells worshipers to be reconciled before they offer their gift, Matthew 5:23-24, and asks which is greater, 'the gift, or the altar that makes it sacred?' Matthew 23:19. Hebrews contrasts the priests who offer 'again and again the same sacrifices' with the one offering of Christ, Hebrews 10:11-14, and says 'We have an altar,' Hebrews 13:10. Revelation shows souls under the heavenly altar, Revelation 6:9, prayers rising with fire from it, Revelation 8:3-5, and an outer court given to the nations, Revelation 11:2. The lamp that burns continually is echoed in Jesus' call to His disciples to let their light shine, Matthew 5:14-16.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses wants Israel to understand how an ordinary worshiper comes to God. The ark and lampstand were out of sight to most Israelites. The altar and the courtyard were what they would actually see, enter and use. The layout itself answers the question of approach. There is one gate, on the east. Just inside it stands the altar. Only after the altar does one come to the tent.

He wants them to know that the altar is God's provision, not their invention. Like everything else it is made 'just as you were shown on the mountain,' verse 8. Sacrifice is the way God Himself appoints for sinful people to come near. Leviticus 17:11 states the reason: 'I have given it to you to make atonement for your souls upon the altar.'

He also wants them to see that worship is meant to be continual. The lamp is to burn 'continually,' and the command is 'a permanent statute for the Israelites for the generations to come,' verse 21. Israel's relationship with God is not a matter of occasional festivals but of a light that never goes out in His house.

Finally, by naming Aaron and his sons for the first time in these instructions, verse 21, Moses prepares Israel for a priesthood that will serve on their behalf, the subject of the chapters that follow.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter prescribed a real altar and a real courtyard for Israel, and the sacrifices offered there were commanded. Those commands are not binding on Christians in the same way. Hebrews insists that Christ 'offered for all time one sacrifice for sins,' Hebrews 10:12, and that animal sacrifices 'can never take away sins,' Hebrews 10:11. To rebuild the altar would be to deny that His sacrifice is enough.

What carries forward is the principle the altar taught: no one approaches God without atonement. The New Testament does not abolish that truth but fulfils it at the cross.

The continual lamp also carries forward as a principle. The church is not given a lampstand to tend, but Jesus says to His people, 'You are the light of the world,' Matthew 5:14, and Paul speaks of believers who 'shine as lights in the world,' Philippians 2:15.

The idea of sacrifice itself is transformed rather than removed. Christians are to offer their bodies 'as living sacrifices,' Romans 12:1, not to atone for sin, which Christ has done, but in grateful worship.

debates.question: Does the placement of the altar before the tabernacle itself carry deliberate theological significance, or is it simply practical design?

views.label: Deliberate theological ordering
views.case: Many interpreters see the altar's position just inside the one entrance as intentional. No one could reach the tent without first passing the place of sacrifice. Leviticus 1:3-5 places the burnt offering 'at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting,' and the whole system teaches that atonement precedes access.

views.label: Primarily practical design
views.case: Others caution that ancient sanctuary layouts commonly placed the altar in the open court for practical reasons, such as smoke, space for animals and the flow of worshipers. Theological weight should rest on what Scripture explicitly says about sacrifice rather than on spatial arrangement alone.

debates.bearing: Both views affirm the same truth, that atonement is required before approach to God. The explicit teaching of Leviticus 17:11 and Hebrews 9:22 establishes it, and the layout of the court illustrates it.

debates.question: What was the purpose and meaning of the altar's four horns?

views.label: Symbols of strength and power
views.case: Throughout the Old Testament the horn is a picture of strength, from the horns of a wild ox, Deuteronomy 33:17, to 'the horn of His anointed,' 1 Samuel 2:10. On this view the horns declared the power of the God to whom the altar belonged.

views.label: The focal point of atonement
views.case: Blood from the sin offering was put on the horns, Leviticus 4:25, and at the altar's consecration and on the Day of Atonement blood was applied to all four horns, Leviticus 8:15 and 16:18. On this view the horns were where the altar was most intensely holy, the place where atonement was applied.

views.label: A place of refuge
views.case: People in danger took hold of the horns to claim protection, 1 Kings 1:50 and 2:28, and the law assumed the altar could shelter the innocent, Exodus 21:13-14. On this view the horns expressed the altar's role as a place of mercy.

debates.bearing: The meanings belong together. The horns marked the altar as the place where God's power met sinners with atoning blood, and so they became the place where the guilty sought mercy. The New Testament applies the image of the horn to Christ as 'a horn of salvation,' Luke 1:69.

study.originalLanguages:
The 'horn' of verse 2 is qeren, the ordinary word for an animal's horn. The horns were to be 'of one piece' with the altar, not attached afterward. Qeren is also a standard image for strength, as in 'the horn of my salvation,' Psalm 18:2, and for kingly power, 1 Samuel 2:10. The Greek translators used keras, and Luke 1:69 uses that word when Zechariah praises God for 'a horn of salvation for us in the house of His servant David.'

The metal throughout the chapter is nechoshet, usually rendered 'bronze.' The word covers copper and its alloys. It is the metal of the censers of Korah's company, hammered into plating for this altar as a warning, Numbers 16:38-39, and of the serpent Moses lifted up in the wilderness, Numbers 21:9, which Jesus applies to His own lifting up, John 3:14.

The 'courtyard' of verse 9 is chatser, a word used for enclosed courts and also for villages and settlements. It becomes the vocabulary of longing in the Psalms, 'My soul longs, even faints, for the courts of the LORD,' Psalm 84:2, and 'better is one day in Your courts than a thousand elsewhere,' Psalm 84:10.

Verse 20 calls for oil katit, 'pressed' or 'beaten.' The verb katat means to crush or beat fine. The oil was produced by beating or crushing the olives, which yields the clearest oil. The same description is used for the oil of the daily offering, Exodus 29:40.

The phrase 'to keep the lamps burning' is literally 'to cause a lamp to go up,' using the verb alah, 'to go up' or 'ascend.' The same verb gives its name to the burnt offering, olah, the offering that 'goes up' in smoke. The lamp inside and the sacrifice outside are described with the same movement: both rise before God.

In verse 21 the sanctuary is called the 'Tent of Meeting,' ohel mo'ed, the first time the phrase appears in the Bible. Mo'ed comes from a root meaning to appoint or meet, the root behind God's promise, 'I will meet with you there,' Exodus 25:22, and 'where I will meet you to speak with you,' Exodus 29:42. The name of the tent is a promise.

Finally, the lamp is to burn 'from evening until morning' as 'a permanent statute,' chuqqat olam. The word olam describes duration without a foreseen end. Its tamid rhythm is shared by the daily burnt offering, Exodus 29:42, the incense, Exodus 30:8, and the altar fire, Leviticus 6:13, so the whole sanctuary kept one unbroken pulse of worship. The Greek word for altar in Hebrews 13:10, thusiasterion, simply means 'place of sacrifice.'

typology.type: The bronze altar of burnt offering, Exodus 27:1-8
typology.fulfillment: The altar was where the blood of sacrifices was thrown and their bodies burned, day after day, Exodus 29:38-42. Hebrews says, 'We have an altar from which those who serve at the tabernacle have no right to eat,' and explains that Jesus 'suffered outside the city gate, to sanctify the people by His own blood,' Hebrews 13:10-12. The cross is the altar of the new covenant, and Christ is both priest and sacrifice, Hebrews 7:27. The type falls short in repetition: the bronze altar never stopped needing fresh offerings, but Christ 'offered for all time one sacrifice for sins,' Hebrews 10:12.

typology.type: The horns of the altar as a place of refuge, Exodus 27:2
typology.fulfillment: Adonijah and Joab ran to the horns of the altar and took hold of them to claim mercy, 1 Kings 1:50 and 2:28. The altar sheltered the innocent but not the deliberate murderer, Exodus 21:14, and Joab died there. Hebrews speaks of believers as those 'who have fled to take hold of the hope set before us,' Hebrews 6:18. The escalation is complete: Christ's sacrifice shelters not only the innocent but the guilty who flee to Him, because He bore their guilt Himself. Zechariah's 'horn of salvation,' Luke 1:69, gathers the image into a Person.

typology.type: The single gate of the courtyard on the east, Exodus 27:13-16
typology.fulfillment: The white linen wall had one opening, twenty cubits wide, embroidered in the colours of the veil. There was no other way in. Jesus says, 'I am the gate. If anyone enters through Me, he will be saved,' John 10:9, and 'No one comes to the Father except through Me,' John 14:6. The Gospel does not tie these sayings to the tabernacle, so this is an echo rather than a declared type. But the shape is the same: one way in, wide enough for all who come, leading first to the place of sacrifice.

typology.type: The lamp kept burning continually, Exodus 27:20-21
typology.fulfillment: Priests tended the lamp every evening with pure beaten oil so that God's house was never dark. Revelation shows the risen Christ walking 'among the seven golden lampstands,' His churches, Revelation 2:1, like a priest tending lamps, and warning that a lamp can be removed, Revelation 2:5. Zechariah's vision links the lamp's oil with God's Spirit, Zechariah 4:2-6. The type reaches its end in the city where God's servants 'will have no need for the light of a lamp,' because 'the Lord God will shine on them,' Revelation 22:5.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ first through the altar. Every sacrifice offered on it pointed to a problem it could not finally solve. Hebrews is blunt: 'Day after day every priest stands to minister and to offer again and again the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins,' Hebrews 10:11. Then it turns: 'But when this Priest had offered for all time one sacrifice for sins, He sat down at the right hand of God,' Hebrews 10:12. The priests at the bronze altar never sat down; no seat is listed among the furnishings of the court, and the work was never finished. Christ sits because His work is done.

Hebrews goes further and applies the language of the altar to the cross itself. 'We have an altar,' Hebrews 13:10, and the next verses explain that the bodies of the sin offerings were burned outside the camp, 'and so Jesus also suffered outside the city gate, to sanctify the people by His own blood,' Hebrews 13:12. Christ is not placed on a bronze altar inside a courtyard but crucified outside the city. The true altar stands where the old system would have called unclean.

John the Baptist's first words about Jesus draw on the same world: 'Look, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!' John 1:29. Two lambs a day were offered on the bronze altar, Exodus 29:38-39. The Lamb John names takes away sin once.

The chapter leads to Christ through the horns of refuge. The guilty grasped the altar's horns and hoped for mercy. Believers are those 'who have fled to take hold of the hope set before us,' Hebrews 6:18, and that hope is anchored where Jesus has gone, behind the curtain, Hebrews 6:19-20. The One who gives refuge is the sacrifice Himself.

It leads to Christ through the one gate. The court had a single entrance. Jesus declares, 'I am the gate,' John 10:9. Paul adds that through Christ those who were 'far away have been brought near through the blood of Christ,' Ephesians 2:13.

And it leads to Christ through the continual lamp. The priests tended it every night. Christ 'always lives to intercede' for those who draw near through Him, Hebrews 7:25, a priestly ministry that never lapses.

A caution belongs here. Scripture does not assign meanings to the bronze grate, the meat forks or the silver bands, and those details should not be forced. The strong links are the ones the New Testament itself draws: the altar, the once for all sacrifice, and the access it opens.
study.god:
This chapter shows a God who provides the means of His own approach. He does not wait for Israel to work out how to satisfy Him. He designs the altar, specifies its size and materials, and says it must be made 'just as you were shown on the mountain,' verse 8. Leviticus 17:11 states it plainly: 'I have given it to you to make atonement for your souls upon the altar.' Atonement is God's gift before it is Israel's offering.

He is a holy God whose holiness cannot be approached casually. The linen wall, five cubits high, kept the court separate from the camp. The one gate, the bronze altar and the fire that never went out, Leviticus 6:13, all said that sin must be dealt with before a person could come near. The same God later struck down Nadab and Abihu when they offered fire He had not commanded, Leviticus 10:1-2. Holiness is not an abstraction in this chapter; it is built into the architecture.

He is also a merciful God. The altar was not only a place of death but of acceptance. The burnt offering was 'a pleasing aroma to the LORD,' Leviticus 1:9, and the worshiper's hand on its head meant it was 'accepted on his behalf to make atonement for him,' Leviticus 1:4. The horns of the altar became a place where the desperate grasped for mercy. The same altar that declared God's justice also displayed His willingness to receive.

He is a God of constancy. The lamp burns 'continually,' the altar fire is never extinguished, and the offerings are 'regular' from morning to evening. God's presence among His people is not intermittent, and He calls for worship that matches His faithfulness.

He is a God who welcomes. The courtyard gate was wide, twenty cubits, and it faced the sunrise. It was coloured like the veil, as though the beauty of the inner sanctuary was already reaching out to the edge. The psalmists sensed this: 'Blessed is the one You choose and bring near to dwell in Your courts!' Psalm 65:4.

And He is a God who appoints mediators. The chapter ends by naming Aaron and his sons. God will be approached through priests He chooses and consecrates, Exodus 29:44, preparing for the Priest He would one day provide.

For worship, the chapter calls believers to come with thanksgiving through the gate God has opened, to rest on the one sacrifice He has accepted, and to keep their love for Him burning, not as a duty that might lapse, but as a light that He Himself sustains.

crossReferences.note: Before the tabernacle, God commanded 'an altar of earth' or of uncut stones, with no steps. The bronze altar of Exodus 27 is a portable and more elaborate version of the same idea: God chooses how He is approached, and human craft must not take over the place of sacrifice.

Two lambs are to be offered on the altar every day, one in the morning and one at twilight, as a regular burnt offering at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting. This is the daily work for which the altar of Exodus 27 was built, and where God promises to meet His people.

The fire on the altar must be kept burning continually and never go out. Together with the lamp of Exodus 27:20-21, it shows a sanctuary where worship never stops: fire on the altar outside, light on the lampstand inside, both tended without fail.

'The life of the flesh is in the blood, and I have given it to you to make atonement for your souls upon the altar.' This is the theology behind the bronze altar. God Himself gives the blood as the means of atonement, and the altar is where it is applied.

Adonijah, fearing Solomon, runs to take hold of the horns of the altar and asks for mercy. The horns described in Exodus 27:2 had become a recognised place of refuge, where the threatened appealed to God's protection.

The bronze censers of Korah's rebels are hammered into sheets to overlay the altar as a warning that only Aaron's descendants may offer incense. The altar's bronze covering itself becomes a reminder that God's holiness must be approached in God's way.

Repeats almost word for word the command of Exodus 27:20-21 for pure oil of pressed olives and lamps tended continually from evening until morning, adding that they are on the pure gold lampstand. The repetition shows how central the unbroken light was to Israel's worship.

'Better is one day in Your courts than a thousand elsewhere.' The courtyard of Exodus 27:9-19, a simple enclosure of linen, becomes the object of deep longing, because it is the place where God's people are welcomed into His presence.

Every priest stands daily offering the same sacrifices that can never take away sins, but Christ offered one sacrifice for all time and sat down. The bronze altar of Exodus 27 and its endless offerings are contrasted with a sacrifice that is finished.

'We have an altar,' and Jesus suffered outside the city gate to sanctify the people by His own blood. Hebrews treats the cross as the altar of the new covenant, standing outside the camp, beyond the courtyard the old altar occupied.

Jesus says, 'I am the gate. If anyone enters through Me, he will be saved.' The court of Exodus 27 had one gate facing east. Jesus is not drawing on the tabernacle directly here, but He claims the same exclusive role: there is one way in, and He is it.

In the new creation there is 'no need for the light of a lamp or of the sun,' because the Lord God shines on His people. The lamp tended every night in Exodus 27:20-21 gives way to the unmediated light of God Himself.

study.oneStory:
The first altar in the Bible belongs to Noah, who offered burnt offerings after the flood, and God smelled 'the pleasing aroma' and promised never again to curse the ground, Genesis 8:20-21. Abraham, Isaac and Jacob built altars wherever God met them. Exodus 27 gathers that long practice into one appointed altar at the entrance to God's dwelling. The question it answers is how people outside Eden, under the curse, can come near to God at all. The answer is by sacrifice He provides.

It builds on the Passover. Israel had been spared in Egypt by the blood of a lamb, Exodus 12. Now the daily lambs on the bronze altar keep that pattern alive, morning and evening, Exodus 29:38-39. It also looks back to Sinai, where blood was thrown on an altar to seal the covenant, Exodus 24:6.

It sets up the rest of Israel's worship. Leviticus will fill out the offerings made on this altar. Solomon will build a larger one. The prophets will warn that sacrifice without obedience is empty, and Amos will see the horns of false altars cut off. Daniel will foresee a day when 'His daily sacrifice' is removed, Daniel 8:11. The altar's constant need for fresh blood raised a question the Old Testament could not answer by itself: would there ever be a sacrifice that was enough?

The answer comes in Christ. He is the Lamb of God, John 1:29, the sacrifice offered once for all, Hebrews 10:12, and His cross is the altar outside the city gate, Hebrews 13:12. Through Him those far away are brought near, Ephesians 2:13, and His people become lights in the world, Philippians 2:15, while He walks among the lampstands as their priest.

The story ends with no altar, no courtyard and no lamp. In Revelation there is still an altar in heaven for a time, where the prayers of the saints rise, Revelation 8:3-4. But in the new Jerusalem there is no temple, for God and the Lamb are its temple, Revelation 21:22, and no lamp, for the Lord God is its light, Revelation 22:5. The sacrifice has done its work, the gate stands open, and God's people live in the light that never needs tending.

quiz.q: What distinctive feature was made on each of the altar's four corners?

options.text: A horn, of one piece with the altar.
options.note: Verse 2 specifies horns on each corner, of one piece with the altar itself.

options.text: A gold ring for carrying poles.
options.note: Rings for the poles were on the bronze grate, not horns; the horns were a separate distinctive feature at the corners.

options.text: A carved image of a cherub.
options.note: Cherubim were woven into the curtains and veil, not carved onto the altar's corners.

options.text: No distinguishing features were made.
options.note: Verse 2 explicitly describes horns made on each of the four corners.

quiz.q: What material made up the courtyard's surrounding curtains?

options.text: Finely spun linen.
options.note: Verses 9 and 18 describe the courtyard walls as finely spun linen.

options.text: Goat hair, matching the tent covering.
options.note: Goat hair curtains covered the tabernacle tent itself, chapter 26; the courtyard walls were finely spun linen.

options.text: Solid bronze panels.
options.note: Bronze was used for bases and utensils, not as the material for the courtyard's curtain walls.

options.text: The courtyard had no curtains, only open space.
options.note: Verses 9 through 18 explicitly describe linen curtains enclosing the courtyard.

quiz.q: What were the overall dimensions of the courtyard, according to verse 18?

options.text: A hundred cubits long and fifty cubits wide.
options.note: Verse 18 states this exact measurement for the whole courtyard.

options.text: Fifty cubits long and twenty cubits wide.
options.note: These numbers appear for individual sides, but the overall courtyard measured a hundred by fifty cubits.

options.text: Ten cubits square.
options.note: That measurement describes the smaller ark, not the much larger courtyard.

options.text: No dimensions are given for the courtyard.
options.note: Verse 18 explicitly gives the hundred by fifty cubit measurement.

quiz.q: What oil was commanded for keeping the lamps burning?

options.text: Pure oil of pressed olives.
options.note: Verse 20 specifies this exact oil for the light.

options.text: Any available cooking oil.
options.note: The command was specifically for pure, pressed olive oil, not any generic oil.

options.text: Scented anointing oil made with spices.
options.note: The anointing oil, made with specific spices, is a separate substance described later in chapter 30.

options.text: No specific oil is commanded.
options.note: Verse 20 explicitly commands pure oil of pressed olives.

quiz.q: Who was responsible for tending the lamps from evening until morning?

options.text: Aaron and his sons.
options.note: Verse 21 assigns this ongoing duty specifically to Aaron and his sons.

options.text: The seventy elders of Israel.
options.note: The elders had a different role, seen in chapter 24; the lamp tending duty belonged to Aaron and his sons.

options.text: Bezalel and Oholiab.
options.note: Bezalel and Oholiab were the skilled craftsmen who built the tabernacle, not the ones assigned to tend the lamps.

options.text: No one was assigned this responsibility.
options.note: Verse 21 explicitly assigns the duty to Aaron and his sons as a permanent statute.

questions: The bronze altar stood at the very entrance to the courtyard, before anything else could be approached. What would it look like for you to let the reality of Christ's sacrifice be the first thing you bring to mind before you try to draw near to God?
The courtyard's linen walls marked a clear boundary around holy ground. Where in your life have the boundaries around what is sacred to you become blurred or forgotten?
The lamp had to be tended continually, evening until morning, without fail. What spiritual disciplines in your life have become occasional rather than continual?

Aaron and his sons carried an ordinary, repeated responsibility, tending a lamp night after night, as part of their calling before God. How do you view the small, repeated tasks of your own daily life, work or otherwise, in relation to worship?

Every sacrifice at this altar had to be repeated again and again, yet Christ's sacrifice never needs repeating. Where are you still trying to atone for old failures rather than resting in what Christ has already finished?

translationNotes.note: The horns of the altar were prominent projections at each corner with later significance in the sacrificial system, including the application of blood to them, Leviticus 4:7, and as a place of refuge, 1 Kings 1:50-51.
Made with boards so that it is hollow indicates the altar was a wooden frame overlaid with bronze, likely filled with earth or stones for the actual fire, rather than a solid bronze block.

From evening until morning describes the lamp burning through the night; some understand the lamps as also being tended, though not necessarily burning, during the day, since 'continually' in verse 20 emphasizes uninterrupted care more than nonstop flame at every hour.
